name: upscaledb
baseline: LevelDB v1.11.0 and Berkeley DB v5.1.0
workload: Full-table scan over 50 million uint32 records that retrieves the maximum value, upscaledb v2.0.0 (built-in analytical function) vs LevelDB v1.11.0 vs Berkeley DB v5.1.0 on 64-bit Linux, commodity hardware.
claimed_speedup: about 90 times faster than LevelDB and about 140 times faster than Berkeley DB (homepage text, read from a WebSearch snippet of upscaledb.com).
compiler_and_flags: Benchmark driver Makefile in the author's gist: g++ -std=c++11 -g -O0 (driver only; flags for the upscaledb, LevelDB and Berkeley DB libraries are not stated); 4 MB cache per database, LevelDB compression disabled.
tradeoffs: Sorted B+tree key/value store with transactions, logging and recovery, duplicate keys, optional integer-key compression (SIMD codecs) and network access; GPL history: lead listed GPLv3, repo README and COPYING now state Apache-2.0 (APL 2.0). The headline number is for an in-engine aggregate that LevelDB and Berkeley DB do not offer, so they are scanned key by key through cursors.
caveats: Snippet only: upscaledb.com and its blog did not resolve from this environment (WebFetch getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so the 90x and 140x figures, the versions and 'commodity hardware' come from WebSearch result text of the product homepage (vendor claim); no absolute timings, CPU model or flags for the libraries were seen. The matching benchmark source is the author's gist 'Benchmark for https://upscaledb.com' (https://gist.github.com/cruppstahl/dd98144e52ceac2e1df06df1fe7b852b, opened: benchmark.cc, Makefile, timer.h, created 2016-04-04, no results in it; inserts, reads and finds the max of 50 million uint32 keys on upscaledb, Berkeley DB and LevelDB). The workload is not like-for-like: upscaledb runs the max inside its B+tree while the other engines iterate. Versions are from 2014-2016; the repo's last commit is 2021-08-20, and the repo README and ChangeLog carry no benchmarks. The paper 'Upscaledb: Efficient Integer-Key Compression in a Key-Value Store using SIMD Instructions' (Lemire and Rupp, arXiv 1611.05428) was not reachable (arXiv blocked), and per its search summaries compares compression codecs inside upscaledb only (about 40% faster queries for BP128 vs uncompressed keys), not against external stores. ioarena lists upscaledb as a supported driver but publishes no results.

name: UnQLite
baseline: SQLite (Python sqlite3 module, one INSERT then commit per key; one SELECT per key)
workload: Store 100,000 small key/value pairs (key str(i), value i) and then read all of them back, through the Python unqlite and sqlite3 bindings, one database file under /tmp, each test run once.
claimed_speedup: UnQLite (plain key/value API): writes 1.05 s vs SQLite 6.98 s, reads 1.35 s vs SQLite 1.89 s for N = 100,000. Ratios 6.6x faster writes and 1.4x faster reads (derived from page data). Same table: LevelDB 0.38 s / 0.31 s, Kyoto Cabinet B-tree 0.27 s / 0.28 s, BDB B-tree 0.95 s / 0.69 s, so UnQLite is not the fastest embedded store in this run.
tradeoffs: Single-file ACID store with a raw key/value layer plus a Jx9 scripting document store; amalgamation unqlite.c plus unqlite.h. No SQL, no secondary indexes. Pure key/value lookups only, which is the only workload the cited test touches.
caveats: Independent but informal evidence: a one-file Python 2 script (third-party author, gist last active 2 Sep 2020, the matching blog post dates from about 2014) run once per engine with no stated hardware, library versions, compiler or flags, so it is below tier A and not a recognised shootout suite. The SQLite test commits after every single INSERT (fsync per row), which makes the 6.98 s write time a worst-case SQLite configuration (no batching, no WAL, no PRAGMA tuning); the read gap (1.35 s vs 1.89 s) is the fairer figure. Both engines are driven through Python bindings, so binding overhead is included. The gist page itself lists the results table; the page notes that its RocksDB read does not return its value. The unqlite.org page and the product site unqlite.symisc.net (the other seed line, baselines guessed as MongoDB or CouchDB) did not resolve from this environment (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND); no vendor benchmark page or MongoDB/CouchDB comparison was reachable, and the repo README and file listing carry no benchmarks. The two UnQLite seed lines are the same project, filed here as one record.

name: TinyORM (TinyDrivers MySQL driver)
workload: Elapsed time of the TinyOrmPlayground project, 620 MySQL queries, TinyDrivers (TinyORM's own QtSql replacement) vs QtSql/QMYSQL.
claimed_speedup: 'Performance is several milliseconds faster compared to QtSql with the QMYSQL driver ... It's ~40ms faster on TinyOrmPlayground project with 620 database queries'; the same page then says performance is 'very similar to QtSql' because 90% of the time is spent inside the MySQL C API.
tradeoffs: TinyDrivers currently supports MySQL only and is swapped for QtSql at compile time with a 1:1 API; TinyORM itself is a C++20 Eloquent-style ORM that depends on Qt. The official vcpkg port excludes TinyDrivers.
caveats: Weak claim: first-party, one run, Debug build (tier capped at C), no CPU model, no run-to-run variance, and the author concludes the two are about equal. The speed-up is about 40 ms on 620 queries (roughly 65 microseconds per query, partly tuned with KCacheGrind) and is on connection and driver overhead, not on database work. The README's other claim ('1000 complex queries in 500 ms, heavily DB dependent') has no baseline. The benchmark program (TinyOrmPlayground) is a separate repo that was not opened. Category 'database-client-drivers' is outside the six wave-6 categories; the seed line guessed embedded-kv. Last commit date was read from the commits/main page of github.com; the repo shows 5,739 commits.
